definition: To say or do something that makes people feel more relaxed, especially when they meet for the first time.
equivalent_es: romper el hielo
examples: Tom told a funny story to break the ice at the start of the meeting.
A quick game is a great way to break the ice with a new class.
situation: It's the first day of a course. Nobody knows anyone, so the teacher starts with a funny game to help everyone relax.

definition: Something that is very easy to do.
equivalent_es: pan comido
examples: Don't worry about the test, it's a piece of cake.
Fixing the printer was a piece of cake.
situation: Your friend is nervous about an exam, but you took it last year and found it extremely easy.

definition: To stop working on something for the rest of the day.
equivalent_es: dejarlo por hoy
examples: We're all tired, let's call it a day.
After ten hours in the office, she decided to call it a day.
situation: You and your colleagues have been working since 8 a.m. It's late, everyone is tired, and you suggest going home.

definition: To tell people secret information, often by accident.
equivalent_es: irse de la lengua / soltarlo
examples: Come on, spill the beans! Who's the new boss?
He spilled the beans about the surprise party.
situation: Your friend knows who got the promotion but won't say. You ask them to tell you the secret.

definition: Slightly ill.
equivalent_es: pachucho / no encontrarse bien
examples: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.
She stayed at home because she was under the weather.
situation: You have a slight cold and feel tired, so you tell your boss you're not 100% today.

definition: To start studying hard.
equivalent_es: hincar los codos / ponerse a estudiar
examples: Exams start next week, so I need to hit the books.
After the holidays, it's time to hit the books again.
situation: Your final exams are in a week and you haven't started studying yet. Time to get serious.

term: cost an arm and a leg
definition: To be very expensive.
equivalent_es: costar un ojo de la cara
literal_es: costar un brazo y una pierna
examples: That new phone costs an arm and a leg.
Eating out in this city costs an arm and a leg.
situation: You see a jacket you love in a shop window, but the price is three times what you can afford.

definition: Very rarely.
equivalent_es: muy de vez en cuando / de higos a brevas
literal_es: una vez en una luna azul
examples: I only see my cousins once in a blue moon.
He cooks once in a blue moon.
situation: A friend asks how often you go to the cinema. You almost never go: maybe once every two or three years.

definition: To go to bed.
equivalent_es: irse a la cama / irse al sobre
examples: I'm exhausted, I'm going to hit the sack.
We hit the sack early because the flight was at six.
situation: It's 11 p.m., you've had a long day and you tell your flatmate you're going to bed.

definition: To suddenly feel too nervous to do something you had planned.
equivalent_es: echarse atrás / rajarse
examples: He got cold feet the day before the wedding.
I wanted to go skydiving, but I got cold feet.
situation: Your friend booked a bungee jump months ago, but the night before she suddenly feels too scared to do it.

term: let the cat out of the bag
definition: To reveal a secret by mistake.
equivalent_es: descubrir el pastel / irse de la lengua
literal_es: dejar salir al gato de la bolsa
examples: Who let the cat out of the bag about the new project?
Don't let the cat out of the bag, it's a surprise.
situation: You're planning a surprise party for Ana, but her brother accidentally mentions it in front of her.

term: the ball is in your court
definition: It is your turn to take action or make a decision.
equivalent_es: la pelota está en tu tejado
examples: I've sent you my offer, so the ball is in your court.
We've done everything we can. The ball is in their court now.
situation: You've made a job offer to a candidate. Now you're waiting for them to decide whether to accept it.

term: bite off more than you can chew
definition: To try to do more than you are able to.
equivalent_es: abarcar demasiado
literal_es: morder más de lo que puedes masticar
note: Refrán parecido: «quien mucho abarca, poco aprieta».
examples: I took on three new projects and bit off more than I could chew.
Don't bite off more than you can chew this semester.
situation: Your colleague agreed to lead four projects at once and now can't finish any of them.

term: kill two birds with one stone
definition: To achieve two things with one action.
equivalent_es: matar dos pájaros de un tiro
examples: I'll visit my aunt when I'm in Madrid for work and kill two birds with one stone.
Cycling to work kills two birds with one stone: exercise and no traffic.
situation: You need to go to the bank and buy a present. Both shops are on the same street, so you do both in one trip.

definition: In trouble.
equivalent_es: metido en un lío
examples: He's in hot water with his boss for missing the deadline.
You'll be in hot water if Mum sees this mess.
situation: Your brother broke his dad's new phone and hasn't told him yet. When his dad finds out, he'll be in trouble.

definition: Extremely happy.
equivalent_es: en el séptimo cielo / flotando
examples: She's been on cloud nine since she got the job.
We were on cloud nine after the baby was born.
situation: Your friend has just got engaged and can't stop smiling. She's never been happier.

definition: To agree with someone.
equivalent_es: estar de acuerdo / ver las cosas igual
note: Se usa sobre todo en negativa: «we don't always see eye to eye».
examples: My brother and I don't always see eye to eye.
We finally saw eye to eye on the budget.
situation: You and your business partner disagree about almost every decision, from prices to holidays.

definition: Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good.
equivalent_es: no hay mal que por bien no venga
examples: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
The rain was a blessing in disguise: we found a great little café.
situation: You missed your flight and were furious, but on the next one you met the person who became your best friend.

definition: To avoid talking about the main point.
equivalent_es: andarse por las ramas
note: En inglés británico también se dice «beat about the bush».
examples: Stop beating around the bush and tell me what happened.
He beat around the bush for ten minutes before asking for a raise.
situation: Your flatmate talks about the weather, the neighbours and football for ten minutes before finally asking to borrow money.

definition: Good luck! (said to someone before they perform).
equivalent_es: ¡mucha suerte! / ¡mucha mierda!
examples: Break a leg tonight! You'll be great.
The whole cast told each other to break a leg.
situation: Your friend is about to go on stage for her first theatre performance and you want to wish her luck.

definition: It is raining very heavily.
equivalent_es: llover a cántaros
note: Lo conoce todo el mundo, pero suena algo anticuado. Hoy es más común «it's pouring».
examples: Take an umbrella, it's raining cats and dogs.
It rained cats and dogs all weekend.
situation: You look out of the window: the rain is so heavy that the street is turning into a river.

definition: Time seems to pass very quickly.
equivalent_es: el tiempo vuela
note: Versión completa: «time flies when you're having fun».
examples: Is it December already? Time flies!
Time flies when you're having fun.
situation: You can't believe your little nephew is starting university. It feels like he was born yesterday.

definition: To learn how to do something, especially after some practice.
equivalent_es: pillarle el truco / cogerle el tranquillo
examples: Driving is hard at first, but you'll get the hang of it.
I'm finally getting the hang of these phrasal verbs.
situation: Your first week with a new app at work was confusing, but now you can use it without thinking.

definition: To watch someone or something carefully.
equivalent_es: echar un ojo / vigilar
examples: Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?
Keep an eye on the soup so it doesn't burn.
situation: You need to go to the toilet in a café and ask the person at the next table to watch your laptop.

definition: To tell someone something untrue as a joke.
equivalent_es: tomar el pelo
literal_es: tirar de la pierna de alguien
examples: Relax, I'm just pulling your leg!
Are you pulling my leg? You really met the Queen?
situation: Your friend tells you, with a serious face, that your exam has been moved to tomorrow. Then he starts laughing.

definition: The final problem in a series that makes you lose your patience.
equivalent_es: la gota que colma el vaso
examples: He was late again, and that was the last straw.
When the car broke down too, it was the last straw.
situation: Your neighbour has been noisy for months. Tonight he starts a party at 3 a.m. and you decide to call the police.

definition: To do something in the easiest, cheapest or fastest way, often badly.
equivalent_es: hacer las cosas a medias / chapucear
examples: The builders cut corners and now the roof leaks.
Don't cut corners on safety.
situation: To finish faster, the builders used cheap materials and skipped some safety checks.

definition: To make more effort than people expect.
equivalent_es: ir más allá / darlo todo
examples: The hotel staff always go the extra mile for their guests.
If you want the promotion, you need to go the extra mile.
situation: A hotel receptionist notices it's your birthday and leaves a cake and a card in your room.

definition: A friendly way to ask someone what they are thinking about.
equivalent_es: ¿en qué piensas?
examples: You're very quiet tonight. A penny for your thoughts?
"A penny for your thoughts," she said with a smile.
situation: Your partner has been staring out of the window in silence for a while and you gently ask what's on their mind.

definition: To wait until the next day before making a decision.
equivalent_es: consultarlo con la almohada
examples: It's a big decision. Why don't you sleep on it?
I'll sleep on it and call you tomorrow.
situation: Someone offers you a job in another city. It's a big decision, so you say you'll answer tomorrow.

definition: To be ready and eager to listen.
equivalent_es: ser todo oídos
examples: Tell me what happened, I'm all ears.
The kids were all ears when grandpa started his story.
situation: Your friend says she has some exciting news about her trip. You put your phone down and listen carefully.

definition: To have just enough money to pay for the things you need.
equivalent_es: llegar a fin de mes
literal_es: hacer que los extremos se junten
examples: With prices going up, many families struggle to make ends meet.
She works two jobs to make ends meet.
situation: Your rent has gone up and now you need a second job just to pay all your bills each month.

definition: Extremely pleased and happy about something.
equivalent_es: loco de contento / encantado
examples: She was over the moon when she passed her driving test.
We're over the moon with the new flat.
situation: You've just heard that you passed the exam you thought you had failed.

definition: Sad and without energy.
equivalent_es: con la moral por los suelos / de bajón
examples: He's been down in the dumps since his team lost the final.
Winter always makes me feel a bit down in the dumps.
situation: Your friend broke up with his girlfriend last week and has been sad and quiet ever since.

definition: To suddenly become very angry.
equivalent_es: perder los estribos / saltar
examples: He flies off the handle if you touch his guitar.
There's no need to fly off the handle, it was an accident.
situation: You accidentally spill a little coffee on your flatmate's sofa and he starts shouting at you furiously.

definition: To make someone very annoyed or frustrated.
equivalent_es: sacar de quicio / volver loco
literal_es: llevar a alguien por la curva
note: También se dice «drive someone up the wall».
examples: That noise is driving me round the bend!
My little brother drives me round the bend with his questions.
situation: Your neighbour's dog has been barking all afternoon and you can't concentrate on anything.

definition: To annoy someone, especially by doing something again and again.
equivalent_es: poner de los nervios / sacar de quicio
literal_es: ponerse sobre los nervios de alguien
examples: His constant whistling really gets on my nerves.
Stop tapping the table, it's getting on my nerves.
situation: Your colleague clicks his pen all day long. It's starting to annoy you a lot.

term: every cloud has a silver lining
definition: Every bad situation has something good in it.
equivalent_es: no hay mal que por bien no venga
literal_es: toda nube tiene un borde plateado
note: Es un refrán; a menudo se dice solo la primera parte: «every cloud…».
examples: I lost my job, but every cloud has a silver lining: now I can travel.
The flight was cancelled, but every cloud has a silver lining: an extra day at the beach!
situation: Your friend is upset because he broke his leg, but now he finally has time to read all the books he bought.

term: like a fish out of water
definition: Uncomfortable because you are in a situation that is new or strange to you.
equivalent_es: como pez fuera del agua
examples: I felt like a fish out of water at the fancy dinner.
On her first day in the office she was like a fish out of water.
situation: You go to a party where everyone works in finance and you don't understand anything they're talking about.

definition: Very jealous of someone.
equivalent_es: muerto de envidia
note: Ojo: en inglés la envidia es verde, no amarilla.
examples: She was green with envy when she saw my new car.
Your photos from Bali made everyone green with envy.
situation: Your friend posts photos of her holiday in the Maldives while you're stuck in the office in the rain.

definition: To tell someone about something that has been worrying you, so you feel better.
equivalent_es: desahogarse / quitarse un peso de encima
examples: I need to talk to you, I have to get something off my chest.
Tell me what's wrong. You'll feel better once you get it off your chest.
situation: Something your sister said has been bothering you for weeks, so you finally decide to tell her how you feel.

definition: To do something that helps you get rid of strong feelings or extra energy.
equivalent_es: desfogarse / soltar tensión
examples: I go running after work to let off steam.
The kids need to let off steam in the park after school.
situation: After a stressful day, you go to the gym and hit a punching bag for half an hour.

term: have a chip on your shoulder
definition: To feel angry or resentful because you think you have been treated unfairly in the past.
equivalent_es: estar resentido / tener complejo
literal_es: tener una astilla en el hombro
examples: He has a chip on his shoulder about not going to university.
She's got a chip on her shoulder because she was never promoted.
situation: Your colleague always gets defensive and bitter when people mention university, because he never had the chance to go.

definition: What you do shows more about you than what you say.
equivalent_es: obras son amores, que no buenas razones / hechos, no palabras
literal_es: las acciones hablan más alto que las palabras
examples: He says he'll help, but actions speak louder than words.
Don't tell me you're sorry. Actions speak louder than words.
situation: Your flatmate keeps promising to clean the kitchen, but he never actually does it.

definition: To pretend not to see something wrong, so you don't have to deal with it.
equivalent_es: hacer la vista gorda
examples: The teacher turned a blind eye to students using their phones.
You can't just turn a blind eye to bullying.
situation: Your manager knows some employees leave early every Friday, but she pretends not to notice.

definition: To be very kind and generous.
equivalent_es: tener un corazón de oro / ser un trozo de pan
examples: My grandmother has a heart of gold.
He looks tough, but he has a heart of gold.
situation: Your neighbour cooks for elderly people in the area every week and never asks for anything in return.

definition: To start organising yourself and behaving in a more effective way.
equivalent_es: ponerse las pilas / espabilar
examples: If you want to pass, you need to get your act together.
He finally got his act together and found a job.
situation: Your friend always arrives late, forgets deadlines and loses his keys. You tell him it's time to get organised.

definition: To ignore someone on purpose, or treat them in an unfriendly way.
equivalent_es: hacer el vacío / ignorar a alguien
literal_es: dar a alguien el hombro frío
examples: She gave me the cold shoulder after our argument.
Why is everyone giving me the cold shoulder today?
situation: After you forgot his birthday, your friend walks past you at work without saying hello.

term: the black sheep of the family
definition: The member of a family or group who is different from the others and seen as a problem.
equivalent_es: la oveja negra de la familia
examples: I was the black sheep of the family because I didn't go to university.
Every family has a black sheep.
situation: All your cousins are doctors and lawyers, but one left school at 16 to play in a punk band. The family doesn't approve.

definition: Completely in love with someone.
equivalent_es: locamente enamorado / colado por alguien
examples: They met in Paris and fell head over heels in love.
He's head over heels in love with his new girlfriend.
situation: Your friend met someone two weeks ago and now talks about nobody else. She's completely in love.

definition: To betray someone who trusted you.
equivalent_es: traicionar a alguien / clavar un puñal por la espalda
literal_es: apuñalar a alguien por la espalda
examples: I can't believe my best friend stabbed me in the back.
He stabbed his partner in the back and took all the clients.
situation: You told a colleague your idea in confidence, and the next day she presented it to the boss as her own.

definition: A small lie that you tell to be polite or to avoid hurting someone.
equivalent_es: una mentira piadosa
examples: I told her a white lie and said I loved the present.
Everyone tells a white lie now and then.
situation: Your aunt gives you an ugly jumper she knitted herself. You smile and say you love it.

definition: To say something by accident that embarrasses or upsets someone.
equivalent_es: meter la pata
examples: I really put my foot in it when I asked if she was pregnant.
He put his foot in it by mentioning her ex.
situation: At dinner you ask a friend how her boyfriend is, not knowing they broke up yesterday. Everyone goes silent.

definition: I promise not to tell anyone your secret.
equivalent_es: seré una tumba / soy una tumba
examples: Don't worry, I won't tell anyone. My lips are sealed.
"Is it a surprise?" "Yes, so keep quiet!" "My lips are sealed."
situation: Your friend tells you she's pregnant but isn't ready to tell anyone else. You promise to keep it secret.

definition: To hope that something will happen the way you want.
equivalent_es: cruzar los dedos / tocar madera
examples: I have a job interview tomorrow. Keep your fingers crossed!
We're keeping our fingers crossed for good weather.
situation: Your sister has a job interview tomorrow and you tell her you'll be hoping it goes well.

term: go in one ear and out the other
definition: To be heard but immediately forgotten or ignored.
equivalent_es: entrar por un oído y salir por el otro
examples: I tell him to tidy his room, but it goes in one ear and out the other.
Everything the teacher said went in one ear and out the other.
situation: You've told your teenage son ten times to take out the rubbish, but he never remembers.

definition: In a few words; very briefly.
equivalent_es: en pocas palabras / en resumen
examples: In a nutshell, we need more money.
So, in a nutshell, the trip was a disaster.
situation: Your boss asks for a quick summary of a 50-page report in just one sentence.

term: to cut a long story short
definition: Used to say you will tell only the main points of a story.
equivalent_es: en resumidas cuentas / para no enrollarme
examples: To cut a long story short, we missed the train.
To cut a long story short, they got married.
situation: You're telling a friend about your terrible journey, but you skip the details and go straight to the ending.

definition: To say honestly what you think, even if others don't like it.
equivalent_es: decir lo que piensas / no tener pelos en la lengua
examples: She's not afraid to speak her mind in meetings.
Please, speak your mind. I want your honest opinion.
situation: In a meeting everyone agrees with the boss's bad idea, but one colleague honestly says why it won't work.

term: take something with a pinch of salt
definition: To not completely believe something because it may not be true.
equivalent_es: no creérselo del todo / cogerlo con pinzas
literal_es: tomarlo con una pizca de sal
examples: He exaggerates a lot, so take what he says with a pinch of salt.
Take online reviews with a pinch of salt.
situation: A friend who always exaggerates tells you he met three famous actors at a party last night.

term: hit the nail on the head
definition: To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem.
equivalent_es: dar en el clavo
literal_es: golpear el clavo en la cabeza
examples: You've hit the nail on the head: the problem is the price.
She hit the nail on the head when she said we need more time.
situation: Everyone is confused about why sales are falling, until a colleague identifies the exact reason in one sentence.

definition: An obvious problem that everyone knows about but nobody wants to talk about.
equivalent_es: el tema tabú / lo que nadie se atreve a mencionar
examples: The company's debt was the elephant in the room at the meeting.
Let's talk about the elephant in the room: who's going to pay?
situation: At a family dinner, nobody mentions that your uncle lost all the family's savings, although everyone is thinking about it.

definition: To sound familiar, as if you have heard it before.
equivalent_es: sonar (de algo)
examples: Her name rings a bell, but I can't remember her face.
Does the name 'Fluently' ring a bell?
situation: Someone mentions a restaurant called 'La Cantina'. You're not sure, but you think you've heard of it before.

term: on the tip of your tongue
definition: Almost able to remember something, but not quite.
equivalent_es: en la punta de la lengua
examples: His name is on the tip of my tongue!
The word was on the tip of my tongue, but I couldn't say it.
situation: You're trying to remember the name of an actor. You know it, you almost have it… but it won't come.

definition: If something crosses your mind, you think of it for a moment.
equivalent_es: pasarse por la cabeza
examples: It never crossed my mind that she might be lying.
Did it cross your mind to call me?
situation: Your friend asks if you thought about applying for the job abroad. You admit the idea never even came to you.

definition: If something slips your mind, you forget it.
equivalent_es: olvidársele a uno / írsele de la cabeza
examples: Sorry I didn't call, it completely slipped my mind.
Her birthday slipped my mind again.
situation: You promised to buy milk on the way home, but you got distracted and completely forgot.

definition: To start to doubt a decision you have made.
equivalent_es: tener dudas / replantearse algo
examples: I'm having second thoughts about moving to London.
She had second thoughts and cancelled the order.
situation: You booked a trip to Iceland, but now you're wondering if it was a good idea because of the cost.

definition: To decide what to do as things happen, without a fixed plan.
equivalent_es: improvisar / ir sobre la marcha
examples: I don't know what time I'll finish. Let's play it by ear.
We didn't book anything; we played it by ear.
situation: A friend asks what you're going to do on Saturday. You don't have a plan and will decide on the day.

definition: To avoid choosing a side in an argument or decision.
equivalent_es: nadar entre dos aguas / no mojarse
examples: You can't sit on the fence forever; you have to choose.
Politicians often sit on the fence on difficult topics.
situation: Your two best friends are arguing and both ask you who is right. You refuse to support either of them.

definition: Not yet decided.
equivalent_es: en el aire / sin decidir
examples: Our holiday plans are still up in the air.
The date of the concert is up in the air.
situation: You want to know when the new office will open, but the company still hasn't chosen a date.

term: don't count your chickens before they hatch
definition: Don't make plans based on something good before it has actually happened.
equivalent_es: no vendas la piel del oso antes de cazarlo
literal_es: no cuentes tus pollos antes de que salgan del cascarón
examples: You haven't got the job yet. Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
I wouldn't count my chickens: the match isn't over.
situation: Your friend is already spending the money from a prize she hasn't won yet.

definition: To become impossible to control.
equivalent_es: írsele de las manos / descontrolarse
examples: The party got out of hand and the police came.
Things got out of hand when the fans started fighting.
situation: A small disagreement between two players becomes a fight involving both teams.

definition: To accept the unpleasant results of something you have done.
equivalent_es: dar la cara / afrontar las consecuencias
examples: He broke the window, so now he has to face the music.
Sooner or later you'll have to face the music.
situation: You crashed your dad's car. You can't hide it any longer; you have to go and tell him.

definition: To make yourself do something difficult or unpleasant that you have been avoiding.
equivalent_es: hacer de tripas corazón / armarse de valor
examples: I hate the dentist, but I'll have to bite the bullet.
She bit the bullet and asked her boss for a raise.
situation: You've been avoiding a very expensive but necessary car repair for months. Today you finally book it.

definition: A very small amount compared with what is needed.
equivalent_es: una gota en el mar / un grano de arena
examples: The money we raised is just a drop in the ocean.
Ten new teachers is a drop in the ocean for a city this size.
situation: A city needs 10,000 new homes, but the government has built only fifty.

definition: To find someone while they are doing something wrong.
equivalent_es: pillar a alguien con las manos en la masa
literal_es: pillar a alguien con las manos rojas
examples: The police caught the thief red-handed.
I caught my brother red-handed eating my chocolate.
situation: You walk into the kitchen and find your little sister with her hand in the biscuit jar she wasn't allowed to touch.

definition: A small, visible part of a much bigger problem.
equivalent_es: la punta del iceberg
examples: These complaints are just the tip of the iceberg.
The missing money was only the tip of the iceberg.
situation: Inspectors find a few broken windows in a school. Then they discover the whole building is unsafe.

definition: In the same difficult situation as other people.
equivalent_es: en el mismo barco / en la misma situación
examples: Don't worry, we're all in the same boat.
Everyone lost their job, so we were all in the same boat.
situation: Your classmate is worried because she doesn't understand the homework. You don't understand it either.

definition: Back to the beginning, because what you tried has failed.
equivalent_es: volver a empezar de cero
note: En español también se dice «volver a la casilla de salida».
examples: The investor said no, so we're back to square one.
The test failed and we went back to square one.
situation: After months of work, the client rejects your design completely and you have to start again from nothing.

definition: Something that has very little chance of success, but is worth trying.
equivalent_es: algo poco probable / una posibilidad remota
examples: It's a long shot, but maybe she still has your number.
Winning the lottery is a long shot.
situation: You apply for your dream job at Google, knowing thousands of people have applied.

definition: To start an activity or process.
equivalent_es: poner las cosas en marcha / dar el pistoletazo de salida
examples: Let's get the ball rolling with a quick introduction.
Who wants to get the ball rolling?
situation: At the start of a meeting nobody says anything, so the manager asks the first question to get people talking.

definition: To learn how to do a job or activity.
equivalent_es: aprender cómo funciona algo / pillarle el tranquillo
note: Cuando ya lo dominas: «know the ropes».
examples: It took me a month to learn the ropes at my new job.
Ask Jane, she knows the ropes.
situation: It's your first week at a new restaurant job and a colleague is showing you how everything works.

definition: To do your fair share of work in a group.
equivalent_es: arrimar el hombro / hacer tu parte
examples: If everyone pulls their weight, we'll finish today.
He doesn't pull his weight in the team.
situation: In a group project, one student never comes to meetings and lets the others do all the work.

definition: To have too much work to deal with.
equivalent_es: estar hasta arriba de trabajo / estar desbordado
examples: Sorry, I can't help today, I'm snowed under.
We're snowed under with orders before Christmas.
situation: A colleague asks you to join a new project, but you already have five urgent reports to finish this week.

definition: To be very busy.
equivalent_es: estar muy liado / no dar abasto
examples: With three kids, she has her hands full.
I can't take any more clients; I have my hands full.
situation: You're looking after twins, a dog and your own job at the same time.

definition: To be the person who makes the important decisions.
equivalent_es: llevar la batuta / ser quien manda
examples: In this company, the CEO calls the shots.
It's my party, so I call the shots!
situation: In your family, your grandmother decides where everyone goes on holiday and nobody argues.

definition: To lose your job because your employer decides you must leave.
equivalent_es: ser despedido / ir a la calle
note: También: «give someone the sack» (despedir a alguien).
examples: He got the sack for arriving late every day.
If you keep missing deadlines, you'll get the sack.
situation: Your colleague kept sleeping at his desk and yesterday the boss told him not to come back.

definition: To pay much more than something should cost.
equivalent_es: pagar un dineral / pagar un riñón
examples: We paid through the nose for tickets at the last minute.
Tourists pay through the nose for drinks in the centre.
situation: You forgot to book a hotel for the festival and had to pay four times the normal price for the last room.

definition: To spend less money because you have less than before.
equivalent_es: apretarse el cinturón
examples: After I lost my job, we had to tighten our belts.
The company is tightening its belt this year.
situation: Your salary has been cut, so you stop eating out and cancel your gym membership to save money.

definition: To cost too much money (usually used in the negative).
equivalent_es: costar una fortuna / arruinar a alguien
note: Casi siempre en negativa: «it won't break the bank» (no te arruinará).
examples: A weekend in Porto won't break the bank.
We want a nice wedding that doesn't break the bank.
situation: You tell a friend that a short trip to the coast is cheap, so he can definitely afford it.

definition: Suddenly and unexpectedly.
equivalent_es: de repente / sin previo aviso / de la nada
examples: Out of the blue, my old school friend called me.
The offer came out of the blue.
situation: You haven't heard from an old friend in ten years and one day she suddenly sends you a message.

definition: At the last possible moment.
equivalent_es: justo a tiempo / por los pelos
examples: We got to the station in the nick of time.
The ambulance arrived in the nick of time.
situation: You run to the gate and get on the plane just seconds before they close the doors.

definition: It is better to do something late than not to do it at all.
equivalent_es: más vale tarde que nunca
examples: You finally replied! Well, better late than never.
He started studying at 60. Better late than never!
situation: Your friend sends you a birthday message a week after your birthday, with a funny apology.

definition: Over a long period of time; in the end.
equivalent_es: a la larga / a largo plazo
examples: Buying good shoes saves money in the long run.
In the long run, learning English will help your career.
situation: A more expensive washing machine uses less electricity, so it will save you money over the years.

definition: To do something unimportant while you wait for something else.
equivalent_es: matar el tiempo / hacer tiempo
examples: We played cards to kill time at the airport.
I read magazines to kill time in the waiting room.
situation: Your train is delayed by an hour, so you walk around the shops in the station.

definition: Something that sounds easy but is difficult to do.
equivalent_es: del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho / es fácil decirlo
examples: "Just stop worrying." "That's easier said than done."
Saving money is easier said than done.
situation: A friend tells you to 'just relax' the night before your driving test. You know it's not that simple.

definition: To help someone.
equivalent_es: echar una mano
examples: Can you give me a hand with these boxes?
My neighbours gave us a hand when we moved.
situation: You see an old man trying to carry a heavy suitcase up the stairs and offer to help.

definition: Not something I like or am interested in.
equivalent_es: no es lo mío / no me va
literal_es: no es mi taza de té
examples: Opera is not really my cup of tea.
Camping isn't everyone's cup of tea.
situation: Your friends love horror films, but you don't enjoy them at all and prefer comedies.

definition: To learn something so well that you can say it from memory.
equivalent_es: aprender(se) de memoria
examples: I learned the poem by heart.
Actors have to learn their lines by heart.
situation: You have to recite a poem in class tomorrow without looking at the paper.

definition: To work or study until very late at night.
equivalent_es: quemarse las pestañas / trasnochar estudiando
examples: I burned the midnight oil to finish my thesis.
She's been burning the midnight oil before her exams.
situation: You stay up until 3 a.m. every night this week to finish your final project.
